title: Original minimax objective saturates early in training
description: Early in learning, when G is poor, the discriminator can reject samples with high confidence, causing log(1-D(G(z))) to saturate and providing insufficient gradient for G; the authors instead maximize log D(G(z)).
canonical_description: generator loss saturates early in training when discriminator is confident

verdict.reasoning: The gap's core problem — the vanilla minimax generator loss log(1-D(G(z))) saturating early when a confident discriminator rejects a weak generator's samples, and the fix of maximizing log D(G(z)) (the non-saturating loss) — is directly addressed by the subsequent literature. MonoFlow gives a mechanistic diagnosis of exactly this failure: it models generator losses as increasing functions of the discriminator's log-density-ratio output and shows why vanilla/MLE losses are flat when the log ratio is very negative (confident D, weak G), while the non-saturated "maximize log σ(d)" objective avoids gradient vanishing because its derivative stays non-negligible for d < 0; it then generalizes this into a loss-design criterion and validates it empirically. LSGAN papers independently address the same saturation/vanishing-gradient failure by substituting a least-squares objective, with theoretical (Pearson χ²) and empirical support, and GAN-QP offers a partial alternative diagnosis around disjoint supports. The exact "maximize log D(G(z))" trick is explained and confirmed rather than newly introduced, and no paper provides formal gradient-norm lower bounds, so the confidence is not maximal; but the specific saturation problem and its non-saturating remedy are squarely diagnosed, validated, and extended.

paper.title: Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Unsupervised learning with generative adversarial networks (GANs) has proven hugely successful. Regular GANs hypothesize the discriminator as a classifier with the sigmoid cross entropy loss function. However, we found that this loss function may lead to the vanishing gradients problem during the learning process. To overcome such a problem, we propose in this paper the Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks (LSGANs) which adopt the least squares loss function for the discriminator. We show that minimizing the objective function of LSGAN yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence. There are two benefits of LSGANs over regular GANs. First, LSGANs are able to generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Second, LSGANs perform more stable during the learning process. We evaluate LSGANs on five scene datasets and the experimental results show that the images generated by LSGANs are of better quality than the ones generated by regular GANs. We also conduct two comparison experiments between LSGANs and regular GANs to illustrate the stability of LSGANs.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper identifies exactly the same underlying failure of the original GAN objective: the sigmoid cross-entropy loss used by regular GANs "will lead to the problem of vanishing gradients when updating the generator," and its loss "will saturate when x is relatively large." Its proposed remedy — replacing the sigmoid cross-entropy discriminator loss with a least-squares (quadratic) loss — is designed so that the generator receives non-vanishing gradients (the quadratic loss "is flat only at one point"), which the paper supports with stability experiments and an f-divergence (Pearson χ²) analysis. This directly addresses the general phenomenon of insufficient generator gradients caused by a saturating loss.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific solution is the canonical non-saturating generator objective — "the authors instead maximize log D(G(z))" (replacing min log(1−D(G(z)))) within the original cross-entropy framework — and the gap's canonical failure regime is early training when the discriminator confidently rejects poor samples. LSGAN does not implement that fix: it never maximizes log D(G(z)) but instead discards the cross-entropy loss altogether in favor of a least-squares objective, and its motivating failure scenario is somewhat different (fake samples lying correctly classified but far from the decision boundary). Thus, while it solves the broader problem of generator-loss saturation / vanishing gradients, it does so through a different loss mechanism rather than the specific non-saturating-log-D reformulation named in the gap, and it does not evaluate the early-training "confident discriminator rejects G(z)" regime in isolation.
evidence_snippets: Regular GANs adopt the sigmoid cross entropy loss function for the discriminator~[CITE:Goodfellow2014]. We argue that this loss function, however, will lead to the problem of vanishing gradients when updating the generator using the fake samples that are on the correct side of the decision boundary, but are still far from the real data.
Second, penalizing the samples lying a long way to the decision boundary can generate more gradients when updating the generator, which in turn relieves the problem of vanishing gradients.

This benefit can also be derived from another perspective: as shown in Figure [REF:fig:loss], the least squares loss function is flat only at one point, while the sigmoid cross entropy loss function will saturate when $x$ is relatively large.

paper.title: On the Effectiveness of Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Unsupervised learning with generative adversarial networks (GANs) has proven to be hugely successful. Regular GANs hypothesize the discriminator as a classifier with the sigmoid cross entropy loss function. However, we found that this loss function may lead to the vanishing gradients problem during the learning process. To overcome such a problem, we propose in this paper the Least Squares Generative Adversarial Networks (LSGANs) which adopt the least squares loss for both the discriminator and the generator. We show that minimizing the objective function of LSGAN yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence. We also show that the derived objective function that yields minimizing the Pearson $χ^2$ divergence performs better than the classical one of using least squares for classification. There are two benefits of LSGANs over regular GANs. First, LSGANs are able to generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Second, LSGANs perform more stably during the learning process. For evaluating the image quality, we conduct both qualitative and quantitative experiments, and the experimental results show that LSGANs can generate higher quality images than regular GANs. Furthermore, we evaluate the stability of LSGANs in two groups. One is to compare between LSGANs and regular GANs without gradient penalty. We conduct three experiments, including Gaussian mixture distribution, difficult architectures, and a newly proposed method --- datasets with small variability, to illustrate the stability of LSGANs. The other one is to compare between LSGANs with gradient penalty (LSGANs-GP) and WGANs with gradient penalty (WGANs-GP). The experimental results show that LSGANs-GP succeed in training for all the difficult architectures used in WGANs-GP, including 101-layer ResNet.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly tackles the gap's underlying problem — the generator loss saturating/vanishing early in training — and proposes an alternative objective to fix it. It notes that the original paper pointed out M-GANs (minimax loss log(1-D(G(z)))) saturates at the early stage, and argues that both the minimax and non-saturating losses cause vanishing gradients for some fake samples; it proposes Least Squares GANs (LSGANs), whose least-squares generator loss penalizes confidently-rejected samples and stays flat at only one point, thereby providing sustained gradients for G. The paper supports this with theoretical analysis (minimizing the LSGAN objective minimizes the Pearson chi^2 divergence, with no zero-forcing/mode-seeking property) and with extensive qualitative (image quality) and quantitative (FID) plus stability experiments showing LSGANs outperform NS-GANs and are more stable.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper solves the saturation problem with its own loss (least squares) rather than the specific remedy referenced in the gap (maximizing log D(G(z))); in fact it argues that non-saturating log-D still vanishes for fake samples that land on the real-data side of the decision boundary. Its non-saturation argument is largely geometric/heuristic — the formal theory establishes the chi^2-divergence connection and reduced mode-seeking, not a rigorous guarantee that generator gradients stay bounded away from zero in the early regime when D is very confident. So, while the gap's core problem (minimax generator loss saturating early, giving insufficient gradient) is directly and substantially addressed, the paper does not analyze or adopt the exact 'maximize log D' fix of the gap description.
evidence_snippets: They have pointed out that M-GANs will saturate at the early stage of the learning process. Thus NS-GANs are recommended for use in practice.
We argue that both the non-saturating loss and the minimax loss, however, will lead to the problem of vanishing gradients when updating the generator.
the least squares loss function is flat only at one point, while NS-GANs will saturate when $x$ is relatively large, and M-GANs will saturate when $x$ is relatively small.

paper.title: GANs beyond divergence minimization
paper.abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) can be interpreted as an adversarial game between two players, a discriminator D and a generator G, in which D learns to classify real from fake data and G learns to generate realistic data by "fooling" D into thinking that fake data is actually real data. Currently, a dominating view is that G actually learns by minimizing a divergence given that the general objective function is a divergence when D is optimal. However, this view has been challenged due to inconsistencies between theory and practice. In this paper, we discuss of the properties associated with most loss functions for G (e.g., saturating/non-saturating f-GAN, LSGAN, WGAN, etc.). We show that these loss functions are not divergences and do not have the same equilibrium as expected of divergences. This suggests that G does not need to minimize the same objective function as D maximize, nor maximize the objective of D after swapping real data with fake data (non-saturating GAN) but can instead use a wide range of possible loss functions to learn to generate realistic data. We define GANs through two separate and independent D maximization and G minimization steps. We generalize the generator step to four new classes of loss functions, most of which are actual divergences (while traditional G loss functions are not). We test a wide variety of loss functions from these four classes on a synthetic dataset and on CIFAR-10. We observe that most loss functions converge well and provide comparable data generation quality to non-saturating GAN, LSGAN, and WGAN-GP generator loss functions, whether we use divergences or non-divergences. These results suggest that GANs do not conform well to the divergence minimization theory and form a much broader range of models than previously assumed.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper argues that GAN generator losses are generally not divergences (even at optimal D) and that G need not minimize a divergence or mirror D's objective. It proposes four new classes of generator loss functions (DM, LM, EDM, ELM), some provably divergences, and tests them on a synthetic swiss-roll dataset and CIFAR-10. Along the way it contrasts "saturating" log(1-D(G(z))) versus "non-saturating" log D(G(z)) losses in terms of boundedness, but only as background motivation for its divergence-minimization critique; it does not study or solve the early-training saturation of the minimax objective.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — that when G is poor early in training a confident D makes log(1-D(G(z))) saturate and yield insufficient gradient for G, with the remedy being to maximize log D(G(z)) — is not addressed by this paper. The paper merely cites the non-saturating trick as known prior work ("[CITE:GAN] showed that ... non-saturating GAN works much better in practice than directly minimizing the objective of D (saturating GAN)") and uses it as a foil. Its analysis concerns whether generator losses are bounded/unbounded and whether they are divergences, not the vanishing-gradient / early-saturation phenomenon; it neither diagnoses when D's confidence causes gradient collapse nor proposes or evaluates fixes for it (log D(G(z)) is already treated as standard practice, and the paper's own contributions are about alternative loss classes and divergence theory). The saturation problem and its resolution therefore remain entirely outside this paper's scope.

paper.title: MonoFlow: Rethinking Divergence GANs via the Perspective of Wasserstein Gradient Flows
paper.abstract: The conventional understanding of adversarial training in generative adversarial networks (GANs) is that the discriminator is trained to estimate a divergence, and the generator learns to minimize this divergence. We argue that despite the fact that many variants of GANs were developed following this paradigm, the current theoretical understanding of GANs and their practical algorithms are inconsistent. In this paper, we leverage Wasserstein gradient flows which characterize the evolution of particles in the sample space, to gain theoretical insights and algorithmic inspiration of GANs. We introduce a unified generative modeling framework - MonoFlow: the particle evolution is rescaled via a monotonically increasing mapping of the log density ratio. Under our framework, adversarial training can be viewed as a procedure first obtaining MonoFlow's vector field via training the discriminator and the generator learns to draw the particle flow defined by the corresponding vector field. We also reveal the fundamental difference between variational divergence minimization and adversarial training. This analysis helps us to identify what types of generator loss functions can lead to the successful training of GANs and suggest that GANs may have more loss designs beyond the literature (e.g., non-saturated loss), as long as they realize MonoFlow. Consistent empirical studies are included to validate the effectiveness of our framework.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly diagnoses the saturation/gradient-vanishing problem of the vanilla minimax generator objective. Viewing GAN generator losses as increasing functions h of the discriminator's log-density-ratio output, it shows why vanilla and MLE losses saturate early (h' ≈ 0 when the log ratio is very negative, i.e., a confident discriminator facing a weak generator), and why the non-saturated loss (maximize log σ(d)) works, because its derivative stays non-negligible for d < 0. It generalizes this to logit and arcsinh losses, formulates a design criterion (any strictly increasing h whose derivative deviates from zero when d < 0), and empirically validates it, including a shifted-sigmoid fix that makes vanilla GAN training work on MNIST and FID comparisons across generator losses.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper gives a mechanistic/analytical explanation of the saturation and a loss-design recipe, with empirical validation, but it does not supply formal guarantees — no gradient-norm lower bounds, convergence rates, or proofs that the proposed alternative losses avoid saturation in general; the evidence for the new losses (logit, arcsinh, shifted sigmoid) is empirical (2D Gaussians, FID tables, MNIST visualizations). It also does not itself introduce the non-saturated fix (which is prior work by Goodfellow et al.); it explains and extends it. If the validator expects a rigorous, guaranteed non-saturating reformulation of the original minimax objective, that formal part remains open.
evidence_snippets: It is known that the vanilla loss and the MLE loss suffer from the gradient vanishing problem in practice [CITE:goodfellow2016nips]. At the initial training steps, the generator is weak which means the associated $p_g$ is far away from $\pd$. If the discriminator is too good, the estimated log ratio can be extremely small, i.e., $d(\rvx) = \log \big[{\pd(\rvx)}/{p_g(\rvx)}\big] \ll 0$ ... the curves of the vanilla loss and the MLE loss are fairly flat when $d(\rvx)\ll0$, which means the derivative $h'(\cdot)$ is nearly zero.
The NS loss, the logit loss and the arcsinh loss avoid gradient vanishing simply because they have non nearly zero derivatives when $d(\rvx)<0$ despite that the NS loss is flat when $d(\rvx)>0$.

MonoFlow can work with any strictly increasing mappings of the log density ratio and this mapping's derivative should deviate from zero when the $d(\rvx) < 0$ to better avoid too small rescaled vector fields (gradient vanishing).

paper.title: GAN-QP: A Novel GAN Framework without Gradient Vanishing and Lipschitz Constraint
paper.abstract: We know SGAN may have a risk of gradient vanishing. A significant improvement is WGAN, with the help of 1-Lipschitz constraint on discriminator to prevent from gradient vanishing. Is there any GAN having no gradient vanishing and no 1-Lipschitz constraint on discriminator? We do find one, called GAN-QP. To construct a new framework of Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) usually includes three steps: 1. choose a probability divergence; 2. convert it into a dual form; 3. play a min-max game. In this articles, we demonstrate that the first step is not necessary. We can analyse the property of divergence and even construct new divergence in dual space directly. As a reward, we obtain a simpler alternative of WGAN: GAN-QP. We demonstrate that GAN-QP have a better performance than WGAN in theory and practice.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly addresses the underlying problem of generator gradient saturation/vanishing in GAN training. It identifies the saturating SGAN minimax loss log(1-σ(T(x))), notes that the usual remedy is to swap it for a non-saturating surrogate such as -log σ(T(x)) (= log D(G(z))), and then proposes an alternative: a new quadratic-potential divergence (QP-div) whose induced generator loss T(x_r)-T(x_f) stays non-vanishing even when real and fake distributions are essentially disjoint. It shows QP-div gives nonzero gradients for two point-masses and reports competitive FID results versus WGAN variants.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's specific problem — the original minimax objective log(1-D(G(z))) saturating early in training when D is confident, and the specific fix of maximizing log D(G(z)) — is not solved or analyzed as such. GAN-QP does not improve or justify the non-saturating log D(G(z)) objective within the standard GAN formulation; instead it abandons the sigmoid minimax loss entirely and replaces it with a different generator loss T(x_r)-T(x_f) paired with a quadratic penalty and distance metric. The paper's saturation analysis is framed around disjoint supports (p,q having no intersection → constant log 2 divergence) rather than the early-training/D-high-confidence regime, and no experiment isolates the early-training saturation behavior or the log(1-D) vs log D loss choice. Whether the non-saturating log D(G(z)) trick itself works or how to make the original objective trainable early is left open.
evidence_snippets: However, the loss $\log (1 - \sigma(T(x)))$ is not always good for optimization, so we usually use a equivalent loss, such as $-\log \sigma(T(x))$ and $- T(x)$. Namely, we may adjust the loss of generator for a better optimization, rather than playing the original min-max game.

So if there is almost no intersection between $p(x)$ and $q(x)$, this divergence of them is a constant $\log 2$, whose gradients are zeros. In this situation, generator can not imporve via gradient descent method.
We find that using $T(x_r,x_f)-T(x_f,x_r)$ as the loss of generator is enough. That results the following generative model called GAN with Quadratic Potential (GAN-QP)
